problems.description: app.py regresses from the seed's modular Blueprint layout to a flat single-file app with all routes on one module, removing the separation of concerns the baseline established.

9 convention violations spread across 4 files (PascalCase classes, snake_case functions, non-UPPER_CASE module constants) yield a convention score of 0.67; naming violations in celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, repositories.py, and test_app.py are systematic, not incidental.
Cognitive complexity +59 indicates route handlers grew logic-heavy; task/DB logic could be extracted to the repository layer the new files imply.

strengths: No new bugs and zero duplication added (SonarQube bugs +0, duplications +0.0%).
Uses timezone-aware UTC timestamps (datetime.now(timezone.utc)) rather than the seed's deprecated datetime.utcnow.
Input validation on task creation (title required, trimmed) and a small shared task_json serializer keep handlers consistent.
commit_reviews.summary: Functionally reasonable greenfield task API, but it replaces the seed's modular Blueprint structure with a flat single-file app, lands a 0.67 convention score with 9 naming violations, and adds +59 cognitive complexity, making it structurally worse than the baseline it displaced.

problems.description: Hand-rolled JWT (encode/decode/signature in app.py) instead of a vetted library like PyJWT or flask-jwt-extended; self-implemented crypto and token parsing is a known risk. SonarQube reports bugs +0, but that measurement does not cover hand-written crypto logic.
JWT_SECRET falls back to a hardcoded 'change-this-development-secret' (app.py) so any deployment without the env var uses a publicly known signing secret; should fail fast when unset.
Tokens carry no exp claim, so issued JWTs never expire and cannot be revoked.

Cognitive complexity +32 (largest single delta): decode_token/require_auth/register/login pack encoding, crypto, exception handling, and DB lookups into a few dense functions; decomposable into smaller helpers.

Convention score 0.67 with 9 measured violations in the touched files: app.py, celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, repositories.py, and test_app.py use non-PascalCase classes, snake_case functions, and non-UPPER_CASE module constants.

strengths: Owner scoping (owner_id) is applied consistently across create/list/get/update task queries, preventing cross-user access.
Passwords are hashed with werkzeug.security's generate_password_hash/check_password_hash rather than custom storage.
Existing databases are migrated gracefully via a PRAGMA column check plus ALTER TABLE instead of forcing a rebuild.
SonarQube shows bugs +0 and smells -2, so no correctness regressions or new smells were introduced.
commit_reviews.summary: Feature fits the app's existing Flask/get_db patterns and correctly scopes tasks by owner, but hand-rolled JWT with a hardcoded default secret and +32 cognitive complexity add debt that the SonarQube +0 bug delta does not capture.

problems.description: New modules use lowercase module-level constants (broker_url, result_backend, task_routes, celery_app) which violates the codebase's established UPPER_CASE constant convention (DATABASE, JWT_ALGORITHM), directly matching the measured convention score of 0.67 and the 'Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE' violations.
Celery and Redis broker dependencies are not added to requirements.txt in this commit; the app imports celery at runtime but nothing declares the dependency.
Notification trigger logic is embedded inline in the edit_task route handler; acceptable for the integration session but should be extracted, consistent with the codebase's model/route separation.

Discrepancy flagged: measured violations on repositories.py and 'Classes should use PascalCase' on app.py are not attributable to this commit — repositories.py is untouched by this diff and app.py adds no classes; those appear to be pre-existing or analyzer false positives.

strengths: Implements exactly the session-3 integration requirement: Celery task, Redis broker config with task routes, and an async trigger that does not block the API response.
Correct transition-only semantics — notification only fires when status actually becomes 'completed' and never re-fires on subsequent PUTs.
Solid test coverage with monkeypatched .delay asserting enqueued args plus a dedicated transition-guard test.
commit_reviews.summary: A faithful implementation of the async notification integration that fits the story's architecture well and includes good tests, held back by naming-convention violations in the new modules and an undeclared Celery dependency.

problems.description: Generic dynamic-SQL BaseRepository (f-string INSERT/UPDATE builders keyed off table_name/columns) is over-abstracted for two tables; explicit per-repository SQL would be clearer and drive down the +43 cognitive complexity increase.

Public signatures in repositories.py (BaseRepository.__init__, create, get_for_owner, etc.) lack type hints, violating the project convention 'type hints on public signatures' and dragging the convention score to 0.67.
+26% duplication: identical _connect()/connection setup is repeated across every repository method; a shared connection context manager would remove it.

Discrepancy: 7 of the 9 flagged convention violations (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, test_app.py) are in files untouched by this diff and appear pre-existing, so the 0.67 score overstates the agent's own non-conformance.

strengths: Clean persistence-layer extraction moves all raw SQL out of route handlers, improving separation of concerns
Domain exception DuplicateUserError cleanly replaces raw sqlite3.IntegrityError handling in register()
Schema creation and migration logic consolidated into UserRepository/TaskRepository.initialize_schema
No new bugs or security issues; dynamic SQL is built from class-controlled constants, not user input
commit_reviews.summary: A sound repository-layer refactor that improves layering and error handling and is net better, though the generic dynamic-SQL base class raises cognitive complexity (+43) and public signatures lack the type hints the project mandates — while the 0.67 convention score is inflated by pre-existing violations in untouched files.

problems.description: rate_limit_key re-decodes the JWT on every request even though require_auth already decodes it into g.user, doing redundant crypto work on the hot path

SonarQube cognitive complexity +34 comes from the nested try/except decode logic and the dynamically built cursor_filter SQL string; the concatenated f-string query in repositories.py is harder to read than a single static statement
Duplications +19.5% likely from the repeated decode/validation try-except blocks and the repeated (SELECT created_at FROM tasks WHERE id = ?) subquery in the cursor filter
/tasks response shape changes from a bare list to {data, next_cursor, total} with no versioning or compatibility shim, a breaking API change
count_for_owner adds a full COUNT query on every list call, adding O(n) DB work per paginated request
Measured convention score 0.67 with 9 violations, but 8 of them are in untouched files (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py) and reflect pre-existing project-wide state, not this commit

strengths: Respects existing patterns: reuses TaskRepository, require_auth, task_json, the test fixture/client style, and maintains the existing repository-method signature shape with defaults
commit_reviews.summary: A cleanly-tested, pattern-respecting addition of cursor pagination and user-keyed rate limiting that fits the app architecture, but it accrues measured complexity (+34 cognitive, 19.5% duplication) and a redundant JWT decode — mostly minor, with the 0.67 convention score reflecting pre-existing violations outside this diff.

compounding_issues: Session 1 discarded the auth/items seed entirely and built a bare task API without a user/ownership concept, forcing Session 2 to retrofit auth as a 'feature' with an ALTER TABLE owner_id migration that the schema init has to carry forever after

Hand-rolled HS256 JWT (raw hmac/base64) and reliance on pre-installed packages instead of declaring a dependency manifest — every session had to rediscover the runtime env ('Flask-Limiter and Redis client are installed'), leaving the project one env swap away from breaking
Repo hygiene: binary artifacts (__pycache__/*.pyc, tasks.db) committed into git across sessions, adding noise and churn to every diff

Celery + Redis introduced in Session 3 hard-couples task completion to a broker; Session 5's limiter mitigates Redis absence with an in-memory fallback but the notification path has no equivalent resilience
Session 5 changed the GET /tasks contract from a bare list to a {data, next_cursor, total} envelope — a backwards-incompatible API change with no versioning
Module-level mutable DATABASE + init_db() at import time constrains testability; the fixture monkeypatches module globals rather than using app config
key_decisions: Replacing the seeded auth/items codebase with a minimal SQLite task CRUD API in Session 1 rather than evolving the seed
Hand-rolled HS256 JWT with hmac + werkzeug password hashing in Session 2, deliberately keeping dependencies minimal over using flask-jwt-extended
Per-user task ownership with ownership-scoped queries (get/list/update_for_owner) established in Session 2 — the correctness backbone for all later work
Extracting the repository pattern (BaseRepository/TaskRepository/UserRepository) in Session 4, decoupling all SQL from route handlers and enabling Session 5's pagination
Celery + Redis async notifications fired only on a real pending→completed transition in Session 3
Redis-backed Flask-Limiter with per-user bearer-token keys and IP fallback, plus in-memory fallback, in Session 5
Cursor pagination with stable (created_at, id) ordering and owner-scoped totals in Session 5
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and monotonically: the test suite grew 7 → 12 → 14 → 14 → 17 with every commit green when run directly (I verified pytest passes at each of the 5 commits). Session 1 delivered a minimal but working CRUD core; Session 2 added real correctness (auth, per-user isolation, ownership-scoped queries, proper 400/401/404/409 semantics) with migration-aware schema; Session 3 layered in async integration cleanly with transition-guarded notification triggers; Session 4 improved cohesion by extracting a repository layer that shrank app.py from ~300 to ~120 lines without behavioral change (14 tests held); Session 5 polished cross-cutting concerns (rate limiting, pagination) while consciously updating the list-response contract and covering it with new tests. The agent's session commentary shows consistently structured plans, explicit verification loops, and disciplined regression control at every stage.
story_review.summary: A near-textbook incremental progression — build, secure, integrate, refactor, harden — with green tests at every commit and steadily improving structure, marred only by the Session 1 decision to discard the seed and retro-fit auth/ownership later, plus dependency and repo-hygiene debt.
